title: A flame measured from video is a number with a ruler, a threshold and an interval
summary: Turning a flame video into millimetres takes four decisions: how many millimetres a pixel is, where the flame edge is, which statistic summarises the time series, and how wide an interval to report. Each decision has a formula and an error you can compute.

media.alt: Three stacked time series of a flame over two seconds: tip height around 42 mm with a dotted mean line, width between about 11 and 13 mm, and tip fluctuation about zero. All three oscillate with the same period of roughly 0.14 s plus noise.
media.caption: Reference render of plot class F11.3 with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery), not a measurement.

source.note: Standard measurement science: pinhole imaging, Otsu's between-class variance, sample statistics, the discrete Fourier transform and uncertainty propagation as in the GUM. The figure is the design system's synthetic F11.3 render; every number below is computed on this page or read from that figure.

read_the_figure.question: How tall is the flame on average, how much does it flicker, how fast does it flicker, and how sure are we?
read_the_figure.axes: x: time in seconds, shared by the three panels. y: tip height, width and tip fluctuation (height minus its mean), each in millimetres on its own panel. The dotted line is the time mean.
look_at: The dotted mean line: the flame spends equal time above and below it, so the mean is a centre, not a typical frame.
The period: the spacing between peaks is about 0.14 s, a flicker frequency near 7 Hz. Count peaks over the whole record, not two.
Width and height share one period: a common driver (buoyant vortex shedding is the usual explanation), whatever their relative phase.
The size of the noise riding on the oscillation: it sets how precise one frame's edge position is.
read_the_figure.proves: A clear single peak in the spectrum of the tip height, at a frequency stable across the record, is evidence of a periodic flicker rather than random turbulence.
if_wrong: Peaks drifting in spacing: the flicker is not stationary; one FFT over the whole record smears its peak.
Mean height that changes with the record length: the flame has not reached steady state, or the camera auto-exposure is changing the threshold.
Fluctuation that looks like a staircase with steps of one pixel: the signal is at the resolution limit and the quantisation noise dominates.
must_check: Calibration scale in mm per pixel, how it was obtained, and its uncertainty.
Frame rate stated, so frequencies and the Nyquist limit can be checked.
Segmentation rule stated (method, threshold, minimum area) and shown on a real frame (F11.1).
Number of runs and the interval type: standard deviation, standard error or confidence interval.

terms.meaning: The number of millimetres one pixel covers at the flame's distance from the camera, found from an object of known length in the image.
The ideal camera in which a point at depth Z projects to image coordinate x = f X / Z. Everything at the same depth shares one scale.
A grey level that splits pixels into flame and background.
Choose the threshold that makes the two groups of pixels as different from each other, relative to their own spread, as possible.
The curve that outlines the flame region in the binary image. Height, width and area are read from it.
Height: base to tip along the axis. Width: horizontal extent at a stated height. Area: pixel count of the region times s squared.
Standard deviation divided by mean: flicker amplitude as a fraction of the mean, so runs of different size can be compared.
Half the frame rate: the highest frequency a sampled signal can show without aliasing.
An uncertainty expressed as one standard deviation, so different sources can be combined in quadrature.
A range built from n runs that contains the true mean in a stated fraction (say 95 percent) of repeated experiments.

remember: Scale: s = known length in mm divided by its length in pixels.
Otsu: maximise the between-class variance sigma_B^2 = w0 w1 (mu0 - mu1)^2.
Height in mm = pixel distance x s. Area in mm^2 = pixel count x s^2.
CV = standard deviation / mean. Sample standard deviation divides by n - 1.
FFT bins are spaced by frame rate / N\, the highest usable frequency is frame rate / 2.
One edge known to plus or minus half a pixel has standard uncertainty 1/sqrt(12) = 0.29 px.
Report an interval, not a single number.

understand.title: Why a ruler and not the lens data
understand.text: A focal length and a pixel pitch give a scale only if you also know the distance to the flame to a few percent. A ruler placed in the flame's plane gives the scale directly and carries its own error with it. Place it at the flame's depth, not at the wall behind it.

understand.title: Why a threshold is a model
understand.text: A flame has no sharp edge: luminosity falls off over several pixels. The contour you extract is the place where the brightness crosses a chosen level. A different level moves the edge, so the rule must be stated and held fixed across runs.

understand.title: Why the mean is not enough
understand.text: Two flames can share a mean height of 52 mm and differ tenfold in flicker. Mean, spread and frequency answer three different questions, and each has its own uncertainty.

steps.title: From pixels to millimetres
steps.note: A ruler of length L covers N pixels, so one pixel is s millimetres. A distance of N_H pixels is then s N_H millimetres. This holds only for points at the ruler's depth.

steps.title: Why the scale depends on depth (pinhole)
steps.note: x is the image coordinate, p the pixel pitch. The scale is proportional to the depth Z, so a ruler 3 cm behind a flame 1.5 m from the lens biases every length by 2 percent. Verified symbolically; lens distortion is ignored here.

steps.title: Otsu: split the histogram where the groups differ most
steps.note: w are the fractions of pixels below and above the threshold t, mu and sigma their mean and spread. The total variance is fixed by the image, so maximising the between-class term is the same as minimising the within-class term. Verified symbolically, with w_1 = 1 - w_0.

steps.title: Height, width and area from the binary image
steps.note: Tip and base come from the contour, the area from counting pixels. Define each quantity before you measure it: a tip at a threshold of 50 percent is a different number from the tip at 10 percent.

steps.title: Statistics of the time series
steps.note: The n - 1 corrects for using the same data to find the mean. The CV is the flicker amplitude as a fraction of the mean flame height.

steps.title: The flicker frequency from the FFT
steps.note: N frames at frame rate f_fps give bins spaced 1/(record length) apart, so a 20 s record resolves 0.05 Hz and a 1 s record only 1 Hz. Verified on a synthetic 3.1 Hz signal sampled at 24 fps: the peak lands on 3.10 Hz. Subtract the mean first or bin 0 dominates.

steps.title: Uncertainty of one pixel measurement
steps.note: An edge known only to the nearest pixel is uniform on plus or minus half a pixel (a rectangular distribution, GUM type B). Two independent edges add in quadrature, giving 0.41 px for a height. Verified symbolically.

steps.title: Propagate the calibration error too
steps.note: H = L N_H / N, a product and quotient, so relative uncertainties combine in quadrature. The ruler's own length is taken as exact here; if it is not, add its relative term.

steps.title: Across runs: why you report an interval
steps.note: Run-to-run scatter is usually far larger than the pixel error above, and it only shrinks as one over the square root of the number of runs. With n = 5 the Student factor is 2.776 (Student 1908), not 1.96. A single number hides all of this.

worked.title: One flame height, from pixels to a reported interval
worked.problem: A 100 mm ruler spans 412 px in the flame's plane. The tip-to-base distance in one frame is 215 px. Five runs give mean heights 52.2, 51.1, 53.0, 52.6 and 50.9 mm. Report the height with its pixel uncertainty and the run-to-run interval.

solution.text: Scale and height of one frame.
Pixel and calibration uncertainty: two edges for the height, two for the ruler.
Five runs: mean, sample standard deviation and 95 percent interval.

worked.answer: H = 52.0 mm with a 95 percent interval of plus or minus 1.1 mm. The pixel and ruler error (0.11 mm) is ten times smaller than the run-to-run scatter, so more resolution would not narrow the interval; more runs would.

analyze.q: The ruler is 3 cm behind the flame, which is 1.5 m from the lens. Which direction does the error go, and how large is it?
analyze.hint: A ruler further away covers more millimetres per pixel.

analyze.q: The frame rate is 24 fps and the true flicker is 15 Hz. What does the FFT show, and how would you tell it is wrong?
analyze.hint: Nyquist is 12 Hz; the alias is at 24 - 15.

analyze.q: Halve the pixel size by using a camera of twice the resolution. Which terms of the worked uncertainty change, and which do not?
analyze.hint: Pixel terms scale with s; scatter between runs does not.

evaluate.q: Another group uses a fixed grey-level threshold of 128 for every run, you use Otsu per frame. When would each be preferable, and what would you do before comparing their heights?
evaluate.hint: Camera exposure drifts; a fixed level then measures the exposure, not the flame.

evaluate.q: Is plus or minus one standard deviation of the frames the right error bar for the mean flame height?
evaluate.hint: Frames within a run are correlated, and the question is about the mean, not a frame.

create: Design a calibration target for a flame that cannot be approached: where would you put it, how many marks, and how would you check the scale at the end of the session?
Write a script that takes a folder of runs and prints one table of mean height, CV, flicker frequency and 95 percent interval per condition, with the segmentation rule printed on top.

checks.q: Why does Otsu's method maximise the between-class variance instead of minimising the within-class variance?
checks.hint: Add the two and ask what is fixed.
checks.answer: Because the total variance of the image is fixed, within plus between equals a constant. Maximising one is the same as minimising the other, and the between-class form is cheaper to compute from a cumulative histogram.

checks.q: A 5 mm bolt head spans 38 px. A flame is 310 px high. What is the height and its pixel uncertainty (two edges, plus or minus half a pixel each)?
checks.hint: s = 5/38\, relative uncertainty combines quadrature terms.
checks.answer: s = 0.1316 mm/px so H = 40.8 mm. Pixel uncertainty 0.408 px for each of the two lengths: relative sqrt((0.408/310)^2 + (0.408/38)^2) = 0.0108, so u_H = 0.44 mm. The small calibration object dominates the error: a longer ruler would help.

checks.q: A 10 s record at 25 fps shows a spectral peak at 4.0 Hz. What is the frequency resolution, and could the true frequency be 4.05 Hz?
checks.answer: N = 250, so the bin spacing is 0.1 Hz. A true 4.05 Hz falls between bins 4.0 and 4.1 and leaks into both. The peak is only known to about plus or minus 0.05 Hz. Zero padding interpolates the display but does not add information.

checks.q: Five runs give CV values of 1.8 percent, but each run is only 20 frames long. How much would you trust the quoted flicker amplitude?
checks.answer: Little. At about 7 Hz and 24 fps, 20 frames span under a second, so about six cycles at most, and the standard deviation of so few samples is itself uncertain by tens of percent. Longer records or more runs are needed before the CV means anything.

checks.q: You want a frequency uncertainty on the flicker peak. Outline a method.
checks.answer: Split the record into several segments, compute the peak frequency of each, and report the mean and standard error; or bootstrap the frames in blocks and refit. A Welch average of segment spectra also lowers the variance of the peak location at the cost of resolution.
